title: How they say it there
job: Regional and generational speech; what marks an outsider
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: -NEYO IS THE ENDING OF SOMETHING JUST NOTICED. It goes on what the speaker has this moment seen, tasted or realised. It is not a warmer -yo: on a fact the listener already gave you it sounds as though you had only just believed them.

-JYO ASKS THE LISTENER TO CONFIRM. It hangs a small question on what the speaker already believes. L4-M4's -janayo TELLS the listener they agree; -jyo INVITES them to, and a learner who has only -janayo is pushy in every sentence.

ENGLISH TAGS CARRY NO STANCE. Isn't it and right? attach to anything and mean nothing in particular. -neyo and -jyo are two different stances and are never interchangeable, so the English tag cannot choose between them for you.

DANGSIN IS NOT YOU. Reaching for it is the loudest textbook mistake in the language. Address is by the name plus -ssi, by the title plus -nim, or by nothing at all — Korean drops the pronoun by default and English never does.

EVERYONE SAYS I-GE. The uncontracted igeo-ga is written Korean read out. The contraction is not slang and not casual speech; it is the ordinary spoken shape, and the full form is one of the three things that mark an outsider.

THE DIALECT HERE IS FOR RECOGNITION ONLY. The pool carries southern shapes a learner will really hear. No sentence asks for one: this course speaks the Seoul standard, and half-learned satuori is worse than none.

A FLAT SENTENCE IS GRAMMATICAL AND STILL SOUNDS WRONG. Speech with no -neyo, no -jyo and no geureochyo reads like a form being read aloud. The tags are where a speaker's stance lives, and dropping them is the third outsider marker.

SEONBAE AND HUBAE ARE THE ONLY NEW ADDRESS. The rest of the inventory is bought already: eonni, hyeong, nuna and oppa at L2-M2, seonsaengnim, chingu and saram at L1-M1. This module spends nothing more on it.

sentences.display: Seoul-eseo-neun pyojunmal-eul malhaeyo. Busan-eseo-neun satuori-reul malhaeyo.
sentences.script: 서울에서는 표준말을 말해요. 부산에서는 사투리를 말해요.
sentences.cue: In Seoul people speak the standard; in Busan they speak the dialect.
sentences.literal: Seoul-at-TOPIC standard-OBJ speak. Busan-at-TOPIC dialect-OBJ speak

words.note: Any Korean that is not the Seoul standard. A neutral word, not an insult — a speaker will use it of their own speech.
The Seoul standard — the one Korean every module below taught, named out loud here for the first time.
The capital, and the place the standard is named after. -eseo-neun sets it against somewhere else rather than merely locating it.
The southern port, and the satuori a learner is likeliest to meet. Named so the sound is recognised, never so it is produced.

sentences.trap: Neither city is a choice a learner has to make. The course speaks the Seoul standard throughout; Busan is here to be heard.
sentences.sound: SEO-u-re-seo-neun PYO-jun-ma-reul MA-rae-yo. BU-sa-ne-seo-neun SA-tu-ri-reul MA-rae-yo.

variations.cue: In Seoul people speak the standard.
variations.changed: one half of the pair, standing alone

variations.cue: In Busan they speak the dialect too.
variations.changed: -do for -reul: the dialect added rather than contrasted

mistake.why: The object particle has gone. Dropping -eul happens in fast speech, but the whole sentence is a contrast between two halves and the contrast needs both particles standing.

sentences.usage: Saying where the Korean you are hearing comes from.

sentences.cue: Outside the capital the speech is really different.

words.note: Everywhere in the country that is not Seoul. It is where a learner first hears Korean nobody taught them.
The southern polite ending -ye where Seoul says -yo. Recognise it in the pool; no sentence here asks you to say it.

sentences.trap: Different, not worse. English speakers already grant that accents carry identity, and Korean asks nothing more of them here.

variations.cue: The provinces have their dialects.
variations.changed: the plain locative, and the dialect as the subject

variations.cue: Outside the capital even the voice is different.
variations.changed: the voice rather than the words

mistake.why: teullyeoyo says wrong, not different. A dialect is dallayo; calling it teullyeoyo says the region speaks Korean incorrectly, which is both untrue and rude.

sentences.usage: Warning a learner that the Korean they were taught is one Korean among several.
sentences.mnemonic: Jibang: different words, not wrong ones.

sentences.cue: With a dialect even the voice is really different.

words.note: A person's voice. L4-M2 already owns sori for a sound, so this is the human one and the two never overlap.
The Gyeongsang word where Seoul says neomu or jeongmal. Constant in southern speech; recognise it and leave it there.

sentences.trap: A dialect is not only its words. The pitch and the length of the syllables carry as much of it, which is why hearing one is a skill of its own.

variations.cue: The voice is really different.
variations.changed: the voice as the subject, the dialect left implied

variations.cue: The dialect really is different.
variations.changed: the claim without the detail

mistake.why: sori, L4-M2's word, is a sound in the world — a bang, a noise. A person's voice is mokssori, and this sentence is about people.

sentences.usage: Explaining why a dialect is hard to follow even when you know every word.
sentences.mnemonic: Mok is the throat: mokssori is the voice from it.

words.note: The contraction of igeo-ga that every speaker uses. The full form is not more polite, only more written, and reaching for it marks an outsider.
-neyo on something tasted this second. Said of a fact the listener already gave you, it sounds as if you had only just believed them.

sentences.trap: -neyo is not a politer -yo. masisseoyo states that the food is good; masinneyo reacts to finding out that it is, and only the second one belongs at a first mouthful.

variations.cue: This is really cold.
variations.changed: the same ending on a different reaction

variations.cue: Oh, this is nice.
variations.changed: the shortest form the ending takes

mistake.why: Grammatically flawless and nobody says it. The uncontracted igeo-ga at the front of a spoken sentence is a textbook read aloud; i-ge is the shape a learner should reach for every time.

sentences.usage: The first mouthful, in front of the person who cooked it.

sentences.cue: The weather these days is really cold.

words.note: The window a generational or seasonal remark opens with. It stretches from the last few weeks to the last few years, and the sentence says which.
The Jeolla shape of L2-M6's geuraeyo. One vowel apart, and a whole region is in it. Recognition only.

sentences.trap: This is the safest sentence in Korean small talk and -neyo is why: it invites agreement without claiming anything about the listener.

variations.cue: The weather is good these days.
variations.changed: yoseum topicalised, and a flat statement instead of a reaction

variations.cue: It's cold, isn't it.
variations.changed: the remark with no time frame at all

mistake.why: -neyo goes on the stem, not on a finished -yo form. chuwoyo plus neyo is two endings stacked; the ending is chumneyo and nothing else.

sentences.usage: Opening a conversation with somebody you have just met.
sentences.mnemonic: Yoseum plus -neyo: the weather, and nothing risked.

sentences.cue: Sunbae, this place really is good, isn't it?

words.cue: someone senior to you at school or work
words.note: The person who arrived before you. -nim is added when you address them directly, and the word does the work a name would in English.
-jyo invites the listener to confirm what you already believe. L4-M4's -janayo tells them they agree; this one asks.

sentences.trap: -janayo here would be pushy: it would tell a senior what they already think. -jyo leaves the verdict with them, which is why it is the tag for talking upward.

variations.cue: Sunbae, this place is nice, isn't it?
variations.changed: a plainer adjective in the same tag

variations.cue: This place really is good, isn't it?
variations.changed: the address dropped, as Korean drops it freely

mistake.why: dangsin in place of the title turns a friendly question into a confrontation. Address a senior as seonbae-nim, or leave the slot empty; never fill it with dangsin.

sentences.usage: Checking a shared verdict with somebody a year or two ahead of you.

sentences.cue: The junior uses the dialect too, doesn't he?

words.cue: someone junior to you at school or work
words.note: The other half of seonbae: whoever arrived after you. Neither word is a rank — both are only about who came first.
-jyo standing on its own as a whole tag. It is the everyday checking word, and the piece of Seoul speech southern speakers keep unchanged.

sentences.trap: geureochyo tacked on the end is a question, not a full stop. Said flat, with no rise, it stops asking and starts insisting.

variations.cue: The junior uses the dialect too.
variations.changed: the flat sentence, with the tag taken off

variations.cue: Right?
variations.changed: the tag alone, as a whole turn

mistake.why: -janayo cannot be a question mark. It asserts that the listener already knows, so pinning a question to it asks and insists in one breath.

sentences.usage: Checking something about a third person with somebody who knows them better.
sentences.mnemonic: Geureochyo — the whole tag in one word.

sentences.cue: Dangsin is not a good word.

words.cue: you — and almost never say it
words.note: A dictionary offers it for you. In speech it is a challenge, or a spouse. Use the name plus -ssi, the title plus -nim, or nothing at all.
The Jeolla filler for a word that will not come. It stands in for anything, and it is the region's best-known single word.

sentences.trap: English needs a subject and goes looking for one; Korean has already dropped it. The empty slot is not a gap waiting for dangsin — it is the ordinary shape of the sentence.

variations.cue: That word is not a good word.
variations.changed: the word pointed at rather than named

variations.cue: It isn't a good word.
variations.changed: the verdict with the word itself left out

mistake.why: Every word is polite and the sentence is still wrong. Aimed at the person in front of you, dangsin reads as a challenge — ask seonsaengnim, or the name plus -ssi, or nobody at all.

sentences.usage: The one sentence in the course whose job is to stop a word being said.
sentences.mnemonic: Dangsin: in the dictionary, not in the room.

sentences.display: Yoseum jeolmeun saram-eun pyojunmal-eul jal haeyo.
sentences.script: 요즘 젊은 사람은 표준말을 잘 해요.
sentences.cue: Young people these days speak the standard well.
sentences.literal: these-days young person-TOPIC standard-OBJ well does

words.note: jeolmeun only ever sits in front of a noun. Korean has no bare the young, so the noun has to be there for the modifier to lean on.

sentences.trap: The generational half of this module stops here. Real generational speech is banmal, and this course does not speak it; what is left is the observation, not the sound.
sentences.sound: YO-jeum JEOL-meun SA-ra-meun PYO-jun-ma-reul JAL HAE-yo.

variations.cue: Young people speak the standard well too.
variations.changed: -do for -eul: the standard added to what they already speak

variations.cue: Young people these days are different.
variations.changed: the claim with nothing named

mistake.why: jeolmeun cannot stand alone with a particle on it. It is a modifier and needs its noun; English the young has no Korean counterpart of the same shape.

sentences.usage: Saying how the speech of a country has moved in a generation.

words.note: The -neyo answer to a -jyo question: the speaker grants the point at the moment of granting it. A bare ne leaves the exchange half finished.

sentences.trap: Both endings in two words, and they are not swappable. -jyo asks; -neyo answers. Reverse them and the asker sounds surprised at their own question.

variations.cue: Right? — Yes, right.
variations.changed: the tag echoed instead of the realisation

variations.cue: So it is.
variations.changed: the answer standing on its own

mistake.why: The two endings have swapped. Asking with -neyo makes the speaker sound surprised at their own question, and answering with -jyo asks the asker to confirm their own claim.

sentences.usage: Closing a small agreement, which is most of what a conversation is.

comprehensionPool.cue: Whatsit — that restaurant is really good. (southwestern)
The weather these days is really cold.
Sunbae, this place is good, isn't it?
